speaker: John Carmack
title: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets (#309)
question: In long-lived software codebases maintained by rotating teams, why do simpler, more constrained programming languages often outperform highly malleable ones?
guest: C is derided pretty broadly for all of these security flaws that happen with memory unsafeness and buffer overruns. But there is this underappreciated aspect that the language is so simple: if you know C, you can generally jump in someplace and not have to learn what paradigms they're using because there just aren't that many available. If I'm messing around with something in OpenBSD, I can be walking around in the kernel and understand everything that's going on. Meanwhile, the biggest defenders of Lisp point to how malleable it is—that if you write a huge Lisp program, you've basically invented your own language and structure, because it's not the primitives of the language you're using very much, it's all the things you've built on top of that. I understand the value of that for a tiny project, but the idea of that for a long-term codebase supported by lots of people horrifies me, where you can't touch the code until you educate yourself on everything built on top. When Google made Go, programming language people looked down on it as simple and almost crude, yet it captured that good thing about C: everybody can just jump right in without restructuring their brain.

points.core: Constrained languages limit available paradigms so newcomers understand unfamiliar codebases quickly.
points.note: Accept: fewer language features or patterns reduce onboarding time; small surface area lets engineers jump into existing code without learning team-specific idioms. Do not credit: generic claims that simple code is cleaner or easier to read without linking to limited language paradigms.

points.core: Highly malleable languages encourage engineers to invent bespoke abstraction layers resembling custom dialects.
points.note: Accept: extensible languages, macros, DSLs, or heavy metaprogramming leading teams to build their own sub-languages on top of base primitives. Do not credit: vague complaints about over-engineering or complexity without noting custom language-like abstractions.

points.core: Bespoke codebase abstractions stall handovers because new maintainers must learn local conventions first.
points.note: Accept: rotating engineers cannot safely modify code until they study project-specific frameworks or abstractions built atop the language. Do not credit: generic statements that documentation is helpful during onboarding.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because in long-lived codebases, code is read far more often than it is written, and the readers are usually people who weren't there when it was written. Constrained languages keep the cost of that reading low.

Highly malleable languages (rich macros, metaprogramming, operator overloading, many ways to do the same thing) let each team build its own idioms and mini-dialects. That is powerful for the original authors, but the knowledge needed to understand those abstractions lives in their heads and leaves when they do. Newcomers must learn a private language before they can safely change anything. This is sometimes called the "Lisp curse".

Simpler languages such as Go, or Java in its traditional style, force uniformity: there are fewer ways to express an idea, so unfamiliar code looks like familiar code. Behaviour is explicit and local rather than hidden behind clever indirection. That makes onboarding faster, code review easier, and tooling (formatters, static analysis, automated refactoring) more reliable.

The trade-off is verbosity and less expressive power, but across years of staff turnover, predictability usually beats individual expressiveness.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In long-lived codebases with rotating teams, reading and safely modifying existing code dwarfs initial authoring in cost. Highly malleable languages that permit macros, monkey-patching, operator overloading, or deep metaprogramming invite engineers to invent bespoke abstractions and embedded dialects. Across years of turnover, successive authors layer conflicting idioms onto the codebase, fracturing one language into incompatible local dialects whose creators have long departed. Maintainers lose local reasoning: an ordinary line of code might trigger hidden control flow or implicit state mutation, forcing newcomers to absorb entire subsystems before making a small change.

Simpler, constrained languages trade individual expressiveness for collective legibility. By enforcing explicit control flow, restricted abstraction mechanisms, and uniform idioms, they ensure code written years ago reads just like code written today. Engineers rotating into an unfamiliar module can trace behavior using standard language knowledge rather than reverse-engineering team-specific magic, cutting onboarding friction and defect rates. Simpler semantics also make static analysis, IDE navigation, and automated large-scale refactoring reliable, preventing short-term cleverness from calcifying into permanent technical debt.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Code is read and changed far more often than it is written, and in a codebase that outlives its authors, the people reading it never got to ask the original programmer anything. A constrained language like Go, Java or Elm cuts down how many ways the same idea can be expressed. Code then looks alike across modules and across years, so a newcomer's knowledge carries over and they can trust that the code does what it appears to do. Malleable languages such as Lisp with heavy macros, Ruby metaprogramming, Scala's implicits or C++ templates let each team build its own private dialect. That's powerful for the people who built it. For their successors it means archaeology: hidden control flow, behavior that changes at runtime, and abstractions whose purpose has been forgotten.

Constraints also help tools. Static analysis, refactoring tools, IDE navigation and linters work best when the language's meaning is fixed, and those are what make large changes safe. The main advantage of expressive languages is how fast one skilled person can work. That advantage disappears when people leave and their mental models leave with them.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
In long-lived codebases with rotating teams, the primary bottleneck is rarely how fast a single expert can write new code; it is how reliably newcomers can read, modify, and review unfamiliar code written years earlier. Highly malleable languages—those with powerful macros, metaprogramming, operator overloading, or many competing paradigms—let different eras of engineers invent bespoke abstractions and private dialects. Over time, the codebase fractures into incompatible sub-languages, forcing every new maintainer to relearn local conventions before making even routine changes.

Simpler, more constrained languages trade individual expressiveness for uniformity and local reasoning. When there is roughly one obvious way to express an idea, code looks similar across modules and generations, which lowers onboarding friction, accelerates code reviews, and makes bugs harder to hide behind clever indirection. Those same constraints also make automated refactoring, static analysis, and compiler checks far more reliable, preserving team velocity long after the original authors have moved on.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
In a long-lived codebase, developers spend much of their time understanding and changing code someone else wrote. A language with fewer ways to express the same idea makes conventions more predictable. New maintainers can recognize familiar patterns, understand what a change affects, and review it with less background knowledge. Consistent patterns also make it easier for tools to analyze and refactor code across the repository.

A highly malleable language can make the original implementation shorter or faster to write. But when teams use that flexibility to create their own idioms, abstractions, or mini-languages, each new maintainer has to learn those local rules. That cost recurs with every handoff. Simpler languages often come out ahead because they reduce the amount of knowledge each team must reconstruct before it can make a safe change.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
In a long-lived codebase, people often spend more time understanding and changing existing code than writing new code. A language with fewer ways to express the same idea makes more of the code predictable from the language rules alone. New maintainers can recognize familiar patterns and judge what a change will affect with less help from the original authors.

A highly malleable language lets a team build abstractions that fit its problem precisely. But when each team introduces its own conventions, later maintainers inherit several local dialects, and the reasons for them can disappear as people leave. Language-enforced constraints give successive teams a shared baseline and can make automated checks and refactoring more reliable. The advantage shows up in lower maintenance costs and safer changes, especially where team turnover is frequent.
